name: The supreme state of the Nāths (param pad; alakh nirañjan)

definitions.definition: The supreme is named the 'state' (pada), the spotless (nirañjana), the invisible (alakh), the void (śūnya) and Śiva; it is stainless, motionless, sky-like knowledge and bliss, into which the yogī enters as milk into milk (GŚ 99–100); the yogī meditates on the supreme state 'where there is neither temple nor mosque' (Gorakh Bānī).

relations.note: the Akulavīra of Matsyendra's school is described in the same apophatic terms; the Nāth texts do not themselves equate the names

name: The Akulavīra — the one beyond Kula

definitions.definition: The single reality, the 'hero beyond the Kula', in which all dharmas dissolve like rivers in the ocean; beyond all supports, aims, channels, breath-practices and rituals; neither near nor far; beyond 'is' and 'is not'; the one abiding in it is every god and every teacher (Akulavīra A.3–41, B.52–54).
Kula is the domain of Śakti — the body, its centres and the yoginīs — and Akula is Śiva beyond it, where Bhairava abides at the end of aeons; the nectar is 'beyond Akula and Kula' (KJN 14.97; 16.41).
Without Śiva no Śakti, without Śakti no Śiva; they go together like fire and smoke, tree and shade (KJN 17.8–9); in dissolution Śakti enters Śiva (2.6).
The one Śakti, the Lord's own power, upholds the body and the cosmos; Śiva and Śakti are not two (SSP 4); if Śiva, mind, Śakti and breath are in different places there is no success (Candrāvalokana).

name: Creation and dissolution within the body

definitions.definition: Creation and dissolution take place in the body: the fourteen worlds are principles within it; dissolution runs from action into knowledge and will and into the light of Śiva; enjoyment is below, liberation above (KJN 2.4–9); the supreme is that from which all arises and into which all returns like rivers to the sea (14.101).
The natural state of the mind free of effort and elaboration; synonym of rājayoga and samādhi (HYP 4.4); the measure of real knowledge — until it arises all talk is hypocrisy (HYP 4.114).

The innate principle in the heart, moving by itself, delighting in others as in oneself (KJN 17.5, 17.18–26); the innate path abiding in samarasa, higher than the 'made' kuṇḍalī (Akulavīra B.43); once the Kaula is known the mind is not to be restrained (KJN 7.26).

relations.note: the innate as against the made

name: The made and the innate paths (kṛtaka and sahaja)

definitions.definition: The Kaula path is twofold: the 'made' (kṛtaka), in which kuṇḍalī is impelled by seals, mantras, oblations and ear-whispered formulas, and the 'innate' (sahaja), abiding in samarasa (Akulavīra B.43–45); conceptions, even of the centres and deities, keep one turning (Jñānakārikā 2.20–23).
The Amaraughaśāsana likewise refuses to call kuṇḍalinī's movement liberation and places liberation in sahaja-samādhi (AmŚ 52–54).

name: Innate absorption (sahaja-samādhi): the mind seeing the mind

definitions.definition: Liberation is where, by the sequence of innate absorption, the mind is seen by the mind (AmŚ 54); cf. seeing the mind by the mind in the midst of Śakti (Candrāvalokana).
Unmanī is a synonym of samādhi and rājayoga (HYP 4.3); the mind made void of void, motionless, not roused even by drums (KJN 14.83–85).

One whose mind is beyond mind is liberated here (KJN 13.5); placing the mind in the heart until unmanī one turns back death (6.27); the 'great pervasion' in which one neither hears nor sees (17.16); the fourth mind beyond the three guṇas (Jñānakārikā 2.8).
When breath is exhausted and mind dissolves there is samarasa (GŚ 94); when breath and mind both dissolve one is liberated, not otherwise (Candrāvalokana).
Samādhi is the oneness of equal taste when breath and mind are gone (GŚ 94); the samarasa of body and supreme state by the guru's grace (SSP 5); the yogī becomes non-dual like milk in milk (GŚ 100).
For one abiding in samarasa all is full, the Akulavīra alone; he is every god and every school (Akulavīra A.24–41).

relations.standpoint: the final union as equal taste
relations.note: Vīraśaiva sāmarasya of liṅga and aṅga uses the same word for the final union; each tradition specifies its own terms of union

definitions.definition: The void is the path of the breath become a royal road (HYP 3.3); the mind 'void of void' (KJN 14.84); the principle known as supportless and without elaboration (GŚ 92); kuṇḍalinī is the pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.273).

relations.note: Allama's void is dissolution in the liṅga, which the Vīraśaivas set above Gorakṣa's perfected body

definitions.definition: The jīva is supreme, partless, eternal, called the lord and the all-pervading Śiva; it is haṃsa, mind, breath and intellect; called jīva while in the body, supreme Śiva once the body is left (KJN 6.4–7); the jīva is the person, the haṃsa, Śiva (17.33).
Oneself is guru, siddha, disciple and Śiva (KJN 11.26); the self is the first guru, binding and releasing itself (17.35); himself goddess, god, disciple and guru (Akulavīra A.26).
'You are guru and disciple' (Yogaviṣaya 6).
Mind is tāmasa (restless, petty), rājasa (coming and going) and sāttvika (steady in dharma); the fourth is beyond the three guṇas, marked by nirvāṇa (Jñānakārikā 2.6–9).
The mind alone is the seed, cause of arising and persistence; bindu arises from mind as ghee from milk (Candrāvalokana); in living liberation the mind is the seed and the spotless (AmŚ 57).

name: Bondage as support, liberation as supportless

definitions.definition: Dharma rests on the mind; what rests on dharma and adharma is bondage; support (āśraya) is bondage, liberation is supportless (Jñānakārikā 1.14–16; 2.24–28).

From the threefold Śakti comes the seed, from the seed desire, from desire poison (death); the spotless dwells subtly within the mind; all three reside at the root of the brahma-staff (AmŚ 38–45); desire is longing for objects and poison its dissolution — abandoning both one resorts to the spotless (Candrāvalokana).

name: The body as microcosm (piṇḍa and brahmāṇḍa)

definitions.definition: Everything in the cosmic egg is within the body (SSP 3); the elements, channels and doors of the body are enumerated (AmŚ 11–32); the yogī must know his own body — six centres, sixteen supports, three aims, five voids, a house of one pillar and nine doors (GŚ-Briggs 13–14); 'the swallowing of the body by the body' is the Nāth secret (Jñāneśvarī 6.291).
The fourteen worlds are within the body as principles (KJN 2.4–5); the one who knows the Akulavīra as abiding in the body is freed (Akulavīra B.93).

name: The fourfold: piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, rūpātīta

definitions.definition: Place is the body (piṇḍa), meditation the state (pada), the letter form (rūpa), the aim beyond form (rūpātīta) (KJN 3.2–5).

Eleven centres — genitals, navel, heart, throat, mouth, head, crown-tip, skull-junction, back, with petals of five, eight, ten, twelve, sixteen, a hundred, ten million (KJN 5.25–27); eleven places of knowledge up to the brahmarandhra and summit (17.2–4).

relations.note: different counts of the body's centres in different Nāth texts

definitions.definition: Ādhāra (anus), svādhiṣṭhāna (genitals), maṇipūra (navel), anāhata (heart), viśuddhi (throat), ājñā (between the brows); knowing their piercing one knows the spotless beyond them (Yogaviṣaya 8–10; GŚ 10–15, 60–62).
The SSP teaches nine centres of the body (2nd upadeśa); the list is recalled as from the root (brahma) centre to the sky centre above the crown, not checked.

name: The sixteen supports (ṣoḍaśa-ādhāra)

definitions.definition: Sixteen places of the body on which attention is fixed (from the big toe to the brahmarandhra in the usual list), to be known by the yogī (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).

notes: Membership of the list recalled, not checked; members omitted.

definitions.definition: Inner, outer and middle objects of fixed attention (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2).
Five 'skies' or spaces of the body to be known and contemplated (GŚ-Briggs 13; SSP 2); in the SSP named ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, tattvākāśa and sūryākāśa (recalled).
The knots of Brahmā below, of Viṣṇu in the heart and of Rudra between the brows, released in practice (Yogaviṣaya 17); pierced when kuṇḍalī awakens (HYP 3.2).

name: The ten channels and ten breaths

definitions.definition: Seventy-two thousand channels arise from the bulb, of which ten carry the breath (iḍā ... śaṅkhinī); ten breaths (prāṇa ... dhanañjaya) move in them and drive the jīva up and down (GŚ 16–29; AmŚ 21–22).

name: Sun, moon and fire in the body

definitions.definition: The moon at the palate rains nectar, the sun at the navel devours it; the three channels have moon, sun and fire as deities; the reversed practice turns sun above and moon below (GŚ 23, 55–59; AmŚ 71).

Beyond the nine openings, the tenth door: twofold as the path of nectar and the path of death, at the root of the brahma-staff; the śaṅkhinī-mouth between the royal teeth through which nectar flows (AmŚ 31–32, 69–70).

name: The five fivefold elements in the body (Amaraughaśāsana)

definitions.definition: Earth as bone, flesh, skin, channels, hair; water as saliva, urine, blood, sweat, perspiration; fire as hunger, thirst, sleep, sloth, radiance; air as running, leaping, contracting, extending, restraining; space as passion, aversion, shame, fear, delusion (AmŚ 11–17).

The coiled power closing the door of Brahman, awakened by the fire of yoga with mind and breath (GŚ 30–31) or by the guru's grace (HYP 3.2), rising through suṣumṇā; asleep in the downward four-petalled lotus (AmŚ 60–64); the world-mother, pedestal of the liṅga of the void (Jñāneśvarī 6.272–273). The Amaraughaśāsana denies that its movement is itself liberation (AmŚ 52).
One of the names of Śiva's Will (KJN 20.11); the coiled Vāmā rising from the anus to the dvādaśānta (17.23); the 'made' Kaula path as against the innate (Akulavīra B.43).

Death comes by the fall of bindu, life by holding it (HYP 3.88); semen moved by udāna is the poison-line of death (AmŚ 38); in the nectar-filled body the seed flows upward (GŚ 65); bindu arises from mind (Candrāvalokana).

Nectar rains from the moon at the palate and is consumed by the sun; the locks and the reversed practice save it; the body filled with it does not decay (GŚ 36, 55–66); in the sky-circle is an upside-down well of nectar that only the guru-ful drink (Gorakh Bānī).
Contemplated as white, cool, fragrant nectar pouring from the sky, it conquers death and old age (KJN 5.6–11); without nectar no immortality (14.94).

name: Reversal (ulṭā sādhanā) and the upward flow

definitions.definition: Turning downward currents upward: the reversed practice with sun above and moon below (GŚ 59), drawing apāna upward (GŚ 37), the upward flow of seed (GŚ 65) — expressed in Hindi as ulṭā sādhanā.
The haṃsa dwells in the bodies of breathing beings as the knot of prāṇa and apāna and is repeated 21,600 times a day, called so 'ham (Yogaviṣaya 28–29).
'Haṃsa haṃsa' is to be said always in the body (KJN 13.2); the jīva is the haṃsa (6.5) moving up and down and dissolving at the end of the twelve (17.18).

At the heart the bull bound threefold roars (GŚ 60); purified channels manifest nāda (GŚ-Briggs 101); in Hindi Nāth songs the unstruck sound resounds in the sky-circle; the nād horn is its outer sign.
Riddling paradox used to point to the reversed practice — the woman enjoyed by two (GŚ 56), the inverted well in the sky (Gorakh Bānī).
Vernacular mantras sealed by an oath of Gorakh, effective, according to the tradition, without the Sanskrit rules.
The beginningless Will-power born of Śiva is Vyomamālinī, Khecarī, Vāmā, Kuṇḍalī, Jyeṣṭhā, Manonmanī, Rudraśakti and Kāmākhyā; unwritten and unread, she is Mātṛkā, the mass of sounds (KJN 20.10–12).

name: Perfection of the body and immortality (kāya-siddhi, amaratva)

definitions.definition: The body filled with the moon's nectar does not leave the embodied one (GŚ 66); the great siddhas broke the staff of Time and roam the universe (HYP 1.9); 'the swallowing of the body by the body' (Jñāneśvarī 6.291).
Immortality by devotion to guru and yoginīs (KJN 5.33); the five jewels ending in the destruction of old age and death (17.12–13); the body standing like a thunderbolt with no dissolution (15.25).

relations.note: KJN 6.7 also teaches that the jīva is Śiva once the body is left; the two emphases stand side by side in the text

definitions.definition: By vajra-yoga in the innate centre of the bone-circle a man becomes like a thunderbolt; the body stands like vajra and has no dissolution (KJN 15.7–26, 'paramavajrīkaraṇa').
Yoga is 'the cheating of time' (GŚ 2); the yogī in samādhi is not devoured by time (GŚ 98); when kuṇḍalī wakes time is cheated (HYP 3.3); by preserving bindu one conquers death (HYP 3.88).
Taught as most secret: the mind in the heart until unmanī turns back death (KJN 6.27–28); the nectar meditations (5.6–11).

In living liberation the mind is the seed and the spotless; the yogī standing on the path of death should know this and practise; by this path comes steadiness (AmŚ 55–59); jīvanmukti is a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); 'die the death Gorakh died' (Gorakh Bānī).
Śiva in a human body plays on earth; his touch liberates (KJN 17.37–41).

Liberation is not: cutting off good and bad karma, Veda recitation, the supportless state, the attainment of form/bindu/nāda by meditation, the bliss of Kaula worship with wine, meat and union, the movement of kuṇḍalinī, or an even gaze; it is the mind seeing the mind in sahaja-samādhi (AmŚ 46–54).

name: The four yogas (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja)

definitions.definition: Yoga is fourfold — mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja — with haṭha as the means to rājayoga (Amaraughaprabodha).

relations.note: the same four yogas are the frame of the Dattātreyayogaśāstra

name: Rājayoga as the goal and its synonyms

definitions.definition: Haṭha is a stairway to rājayoga (HYP 1.1); rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, manonmanī, amaratva, laya, tattva, śūnyāśūnya, param pada, amanaska, advaita, nirālamba, nirañjana, jīvanmukti, sahajā and turyā are one (HYP 4.3–4).
Non-harming, sense-restraint, compassion, feeling, patience, conquest of anger, meditation and knowledge are the flowers with which the body-liṅga is worshipped (KJN 3.25–26).
The true liṅga is within the body — the all-pervading one above the lotuses in which all dissolves; liṅgas of stone, wood or clay are to be abandoned (KJN 3.9–31).

relations.standpoint: the liṅga as the site of dissolution
relations.note: Śaiva traditions distinguish the partless and embodied liṅga; the Kaula rejects the external liṅga altogether

definitions.definition: One ever joined in non-duality succeeds; abandoning the attitude of duality one lives by non-dual conduct; the yogī takes fragrance and stench alike and is unstained by merit and sin; forms of conduct (as child, madman, king...) are whatever vow he wills; no one may be made to take the caru by force (KJN 11–12).

name: The Nāth critique of ritual and caste

definitions.definition: For one who knows the supreme there is no caste, sacrifice, fasting, pilgrimage, image or rite (Akulavīra A.42–48, B.93–96); no lunar day or fast is prescribed — rely on knowledge alone (KJN 21.10); the yogī meditates where there is neither temple nor mosque (Gorakh Bānī); the external liṅga is rejected (KJN 3.14–18).
Eating one dies, not eating one dies — one crosses by restraint; laugh and play but do not break the mind (Gorakh Bānī); breathe slowly, neither holding too long nor releasing hastily (GŚ 51).

name: The marks of the hero and the Śakti

definitions.definition: The Śakti is devoted to Kula and guru, fearless and of good conduct; the hero is truthful, resolute, free of anger, brave, knowing the Śakti born of the body and formed by non-dual conduct (KJN 20.14–22).

Nothing is to be shunned as impure; the practitioner overcomes disgust, fear, shame and the other fetters, since one freed from the fetters is Maheśvara (Kulārṇava 13.90–91, cited in Aghora teaching).
Non-dual conduct: fragrance and stench alike; unstained by merit and sin (KJN 11.26–29).

relations.standpoint: the conduct of one freed from fetters
relations.note: both teach non-difference of pure and impure as the conduct of the free; Aghora's own texts not yet extracted

definitions.definition: Disgust, doubt, fear, shame, loathing, family, conduct and caste (Kulārṇava 13.90).

name: The cremation ground and the skull in Aghora

definitions.definition: The Aghora ascetic dwells and practises in the cremation ground, eats from a skull bowl and smears ash, so as to see Śiva in what is feared; details are secret and restricted.
The skull is the best of vessels for the Kaula rite (KJN 12.13).
In Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām's teaching Aghora is expressed as service of the sick (leprosy) and the outcaste and as rejection of caste and social evils, open to householders.

name: The powers (siddhi) in Nāth and Kaula teaching

definitions.definition: Powers arise as signs of practice on the centres: trembling, speech in tongues, levitation, poetry, knowledge of past and future, change of form, the eight powers, entering other bodies (KJN 7.20–24; 8.30–45; 14.15–42).
The eight powers arise in the nectar-filled body (GŚ 65); the siddhas broke the staff of Time (HYP 1.9).

relations.note: powers are signs, but are not to be grasped (Akulavīra B.84)

definitions.definition: The many powers, the nether regions and alchemy, even if obtained, are not to be grasped: they are nets leading down (Akulavīra B.83–84).
Arrest of grey hair, attainment of the desired, taking forms at will, the imperishable portion, and the great jewel — destruction of old age and death (KJN 17.12–13).
Meeting the yoginīs is a fruit of practice and a condition of success; at Kāmākhyā one meets them and becomes their equal (KJN 7.22; 16.8).
The yoginīs move on earth in the forms of birds and animals and seize the 'animal'; women and maidens are to be honoured and never spoken to in anger (KJN 23).

The Kaulajñānanirṇaya teaches rites with meat, fish, wine, a female partner and substances ordinarily held impure, a consecration and vessels; recorded here only in summary, with the text's own limits (no compulsion, secrecy, testing).
Ādinātha → Matsyendra → Gorakṣa, and from Gorakṣa the siddhas and panths (HYP 1.1–9; Yogaviṣaya 3–5); in Maharashtra Gorakṣa → Gahinī → Nivṛtti → Jñāneśvar (Jñāneśvarī 18).

name: The guru in the Nāth tradition

definitions.definition: Without the true guru the nectar cannot be drunk (Gorakh Bānī); by the guru's grace alone body and supreme state become one taste (SSP 5); kuṇḍalinī wakes by the guru's grace (HYP 3.2); the realised one liberates by his touch (KJN 17.38–40); the disciple awakens the guru when he forgets (Gorakṣavijaya).
Viśvapāda, Vicitrapāda, Śvetapāda, Bhaṭṭapāda, Macchendrapāda and others are worshipped by name; Bhairava explains these names as his own (KJN 9.6–9; 16.11–21).

name: Secrecy and the testing of the disciple

definitions.definition: The teaching is kept from the undevoted, the deceitful and the cruel and given only to a devoted, tested disciple, even one tested for a year; the adept keeps his mark hidden (KJN 4.20; 5.35; 6.13–14; 14.4–11; 17.11; 22.6).
The haṭha knowledge is to be kept secret: kept secret it is potent, revealed it is powerless (HYP 1.11).
The Kaula teaching is 'heard as handed down in succession', passing from ear to ear (KJN 6.8–9; 17.10).

name: The descent of the Kaula in the four ages

definitions.definition: The Kaula came down as Jñānanirṇiti, Mahat, Siddhāmṛta and, in Kali, Matsyodara; stolen by Kārttikeya and swallowed by a fish, it was recovered by Bhairava as fisherman; it came from Candradvīpa and is in every house of the yoginīs in Kāmarūpa (KJN 16.27–48; 22.10–12).

name: The Kaula scriptures named in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya

definitions.definition: Kulapañcāśikā, Kulasāgara, Kulogha, Hṛdaya, Bhairavodyānaka, Candrakaula, Jñānanirṇaya, and from them Sṛṣṭikaula, Mahākaula, Timira, Siddhāmṛta, Mātakaula, Śaktibheda, Ūrmikaula, Siddheśvara and the Vajra-born (KJN 21.2–7).

name: The seats and fields of the Yoginīkaula

definitions.definition: Fields: Karavīra, Mahākāla, Devīkoṭa, Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Caritra, Ekāmraka, Aṭṭahāsa, Jayantī; seats: Kāmākhyā, Pūrṇagiri, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda; meeting places Śrīśaila, Mahendra, Kāmākhyā (KJN 8.16–22; 16.5–8).

name: The nine Nāths (nava-nātha)

definitions.definition: Lists vary by region. The Marathi list (Navanātha Bhaktisāra): Macchindra, Gorakh, Jālandhar, Kānif, Carpaṭ, Nāg, Bhartarī, Revaṇ, Gahinī — as the nine Nārāyaṇas. North Indian and Nepalese lists differ (lists recorded by Briggs and others are not reproduced here).

notes: Members = the Marathi list only; variant lists are a gap to be filled from sources.

name: The eighty-four siddhas in Nāth tradition

definitions.definition: The Nāths revere eighty-four siddhas; the Haṭhapradīpikā names over thirty mahāsiddhas beginning with Ādinātha (1.5–8); the Varṇaratnākara gives a list of eighty-four mixing Nāth and Buddhist names.

relations.note: overlap with the Buddhist list of Abhayadatta (U44/U49 treat the overlap)

name: The twelve panths (bārah panth)

definitions.definition: The Nāth order is divided into twelve panths, traditionally set in order by Gorakhnāth; lists commonly include the Satyanāth, Dharamnāth, Rām(ke), Nāṭeśvarī (Lakṣmaṇnāth), Kanthaḍ, Kapilānī, Vairāg (Bharthari), Mannāth, Āī, Pāgal, Dhajnāth and Gaṅgānāth panths, but the lists vary.

notes: Recalled; list to be checked against sources. Several panths claim founders among the nine Nāths.

definitions.definition: Initiation in stages: first the cutting of the top-knot, the mantra and the black cord (the aughaṛ); after probation the splitting of the ear-cartilages and the wearing of the earrings (the darśanī / kānphaṭa), with a new name ending in -nāth; the Gorakṣaguṭikā tells of Gorakṣa taking 'the split ear and the cut top-knot'.

name: The insignia of the Nāth yogī

definitions.definition: Earrings (darśan/mudrā), the nād horn on the black selī cord, ash, the dhūnī fire, patched cloak, begging bowl and the greeting 'ādeś'; depicted already in the Padmāvat (1540).

Principal seats include the Gorakhnāth Maṭh (Gorakhpur), Gorakh Ṭillā / Tilla Jogian (Punjab, historically the chief seat), Kadri (Mangaluru), Dhinodhar (Kutch), Asthal Bohar (Rohtak), the Mahāmandir (Jodhpur), Tryambakeśvar and Madhi (Maharashtra), and seats in Nepal (Gorkha; Mṛgasthalī).
The tradition holds Gorakṣa to be deathless and to have appeared in each of the four ages at different places.

name: Nāth cosmogony: the origin of the body (SSP 1)

definitions.definition: From the nameless supreme its own power comes forth, and through the powers Parā, Aparā, Sūkṣmā and Kuṇḍalinī the supreme bodies and finally the human body arise (SSP 1).
The Nāth ideal of the free yogī who has shaken off all conventions and stands above all schools (SSP 6).

Dattātreya (ādiguru) → Bābā Kālūrām → Bābā Kīnārām → the heads of Krīm Kuṇḍ (Bījārām and successors to the present Siddhārth Gautam Rām); a parallel line through Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām's Sarveśvarī Samūh.
Nāth yogīs (like other renouncers) are not cremated but buried seated in a tomb called samādhi, over which a shrine may be raised.

By casting the breath upward the skull splits and the jīva goes to the spotless and becomes the all-pervading Śiva (KJN 20.1–3); at the fall of the body the skull splits for one who has the nyāsa (13.8); once the body is left the jīva is called supreme Śiva (6.7). Restricted: no method recorded.

relations.standpoint: departure through the crown at death
relations.note: yogic departure at death is also taught in Upaniṣadic and Purāṇic yoga
